title: Universality in randomly connected neural networks: old and new on a conjecture of Geman and Hwang
abstract: Randomly connected networks are ubiquitous in computer science, physics or biology. A central question is whether, and how, their collective dynamics depend on the choice of the distribution of the random couplings. Forty years ago, Geman and Hwang formulated a precise version of this \emph{universality} question for randomly connected neural networks. We come back to these conjectures, review what was proven since, provide a few new extensions and propose new conjectures in this paper. For $n$ neuron networks with couplings with a mean scaling as $1/n$ and light enough tails, two classes of limits are expected. For \emph{weakly heterogeneous} couplings, with variance $o(1/n)$, the network is predicted to converge to a McKean--Vlasov equation, and a broad literature has established this under general assumptions. For \emph{strongly heterogeneous} couplings, with variance of order $1/n$, the limit is a non-Markovian equation driven by a self-consistent Gaussian process. After landmark results for Gaussian couplings, universality was only recently established for linear interactions, while the continuous-time nonlinear case relevant to neuroscience remained open. Here, in the weakly heterogeneous regime, we prove quenched convergence on every time interval under a fourth-moment assumption only, and convergence in probability under an assumption slightly stronger than a second moment. In the strongly heterogeneous regime, we prove convergence for nonlinear interactions in continuous time, averaged over sub-Gaussian couplings and on every time interval, by a relative-entropy comparison with Gaussian couplings. We then extend the conjecture to heavy-tailed couplings, and propose a limit driven by a self-consistent $α$-stable process, for which we prove existence for every $α\in(0,2)$ and uniqueness for $α\in[1,2)$, and provide extensive numerical evidence in all three cases.
summary: This paper rigorously investigates the universality of dynamics in large, randomly connected neural networks. It establishes that the system's long-term behavior depends critically on the statistical properties of the random couplings. By proving convergence to different limiting equations—including McKean–Vlasov, Gaussian, and $\alpha$-stable processes—the work deepens the understanding of collective dynamics in complex, disordered systems.
main_problem: The paper investigates the universality of collective dynamics in randomly connected neural networks, determining if the long-term behavior depends on the specific distribution of random coupling strengths.
main_result: The authors prove convergence to different limiting equations—McKean–Vlasov, non-Markovian Gaussian, or $\alpha$-stable—depending on whether the couplings are weakly, strongly, or heavy-tailed.
method: The analysis relies on extending the Geman and Hwang conjecture by proving quenched convergence, using relative-entropy comparisons, and analyzing the propagation of chaos across different coupling regimes.
model_or_system: The system is a randomly connected neural network governed by a firing-rate equation involving intrinsic dynamics, random couplings ($J_{ij}$), and stochastic noise. The analysis covers three regimes: weakly heterogeneous (variance $o(1/n)$), strongly heterogeneous (variance $O(1/n)$), and heavy-tailed couplings.
key_observables: The limiting dynamics are the key observables, including the McKean–Vlasov equation, self-consistent Gaussian processes, and $\alpha$-stable processes.
important_parameters: The key parameters are the scaling of the coupling variance relative to $1/n$, and the tail index $\alpha$ for heavy-tailed couplings.
main_assumptions: Assumptions include the Lipschitz continuity of the intrinsic dynamics, moment conditions (e.g., fourth-moment assumption for weak heterogeneity), and the assumption of sub-Gaussian couplings for one proof.
figures_summary: Figures are noted to show trajectories illustrating convergence in the weakly heterogeneous regime and quantitative comparisons of network simulations to predicted limits across different coupling scalings.
paper_structure: The paper reviews the foundational conjecture, then presents new proofs and extensions for the three distinct coupling regimes (weakly, strongly, and heavy-tailed), concluding with proposals for new conjectures.
why_interesting: The study of complex, non-equilibrium dynamics in large, disordered systems, such as neural networks, shares mathematical techniques with spin-glass models and disordered quantum systems, making it relevant for understanding emergent collective behavior.
